study_identification_part.si_4_title: Using normative modeling and machine learning for detecting mild traumatic brain injury from magnetoencephalography data

nm2_1_modeling_methods.detail: The normative model was constructed by calculating the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of power spectra across a large reference dataset (Cam-CAN, n=621) to generate Z-score deviation maps. The study compared two approaches: a 'full' normative model using the entire reference dataset and 'age-matched' models using age-decade subsets of the reference data.
nm2_1_modeling_methods.supporting_text: To obtain normative models, the mean μ and standard deviation σ of the power spectra were calculated across the subjects from the normative dataset (Fig 1B). These statistics were then used for converting the power spectrum matrices for the patients and their healthy controls, into deviations maps of Z-scores over the entire cortex

nm2_2_response_variable.detail: Source-level power spectral densities (PSDs) were calculated for each cortical region (binned into 448 parcels) and across six frequency bands: delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), low beta (13-17 Hz), high beta (17-30 Hz), and gamma (30-40 Hz).
nm2_2_response_variable.supporting_text: source-level power spectra computed from resting-state MEG recordings ... In the frequency dimension, six frequency bands were defined: delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), low beta (13-17 Hz), high beta (17-30 Hz), and gamma (30-40 Hz).

nm2_3_explanatory_variables.detail: No variables were used as predictors in a regression-based normative model. The study used group-wide means and standard deviations. In the 'age-matched' approach, age was used as a selection criterion for the reference subset, but not as a continuous or categorical predictor within a statistical model.
